- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Several guest stars were considered for recurring roles on Cheers.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Notable examples include Kirstie Alley, who played Rebecca Howe for six seasons after Shelley Long left the show.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] George Wendt's real-life wife, Bernadette Birkett, played Norm's wife, Vera, in several episodes.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Other guest stars who appeared in multiple episodes include John Mahoney, Emma Thompson, Bebe Neuwirth, and Jay Thomas.
- [USER] User was surprised to learn that Kirstie Alley was originally a guest star on Cheers.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kirstie Alley joined the cast of Cheers in season 6 after Shelley Long left the show.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] She played the character Rebecca Howe, who was initially hired as the manager of Cheers by Sam Malone.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kirstie Alley's performance was well-received by audiences and critics.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kirstie Alley became a significant part of the show's cast for the next six seasons.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kirstie Alley won an Emmy Award for her role in 1991.
- [USER] User finds it fascinating to learn about the behind-the-scenes of a TV show.
- [USER] User inquired about interesting facts about the Cheers set.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The "Cheers" sign that hung outside the bar was actually a real sign from a neighborhood bar in Boston.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The iconic Cheers bar was built on a soundstage in Hollywood, not in Boston.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The bar was designed after a real Boston bar, the Bull & Finch Pub, which still exists today.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The set included a replica of the famous Cheers pool table, designed to look like a pool table from the 1890s.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The bar set was so accurate that fans would often write letters to the fictional Cheers bar, thinking it was a real place.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The front door of the bar was intentionally squeaky, to allow for comedic timing during the show's dialogue.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The set designers created a "walk-and-talk" section of the bar for characters to move through while talking, which became a signature feature of the show.
